newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Wheels of new Europe to start rolling in Sweden.
newsitem.headline: Wheels of new Europe to start rolling in Sweden.

text.p: The new centre-left Europe, dizzy from recent election victories, will assemble in Sweden this Thursday with Britain and France's new premiers in the spotlight while new relationships form in the wings.
Although 13 of the 15 European Union (EU) countries now have Socialist or Social Democratic governments, the ideological spread of the centre-left remains wide.

The European Social Democratic Parties (ESP) Congress in Malmo, attended by nine EU prime ministers including newcomers Tony Blair from Britain and France's Lionel Jospin, offers a chance to meet before an EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
"This is a very important meeting place, under the slogan 'Our responsibility: a new Europe'," Roger Hallhag, EPS assistant international secretary, told Reuters.
"The agenda is not so advanced...but we will form a consensus here on broad national differences.
"We are providing a meeting place for like-minded political leaders in Europe and giving them a chance to sort things out."

Sweeping election victories for Britain's Labour Party on May 1 and for France's Socialist Party last weekend have left just Germany and Spain with conservative administrations in Europe, boosting hopes for a closer, more unified continent.
"The change in Britain has definitely created a better atmosphere in Europe than there used to be but we are still waiting for the hardware," said one Western diplomat.

While the three day congress attended by 1,000 people will focus on Europe's future direction, it will give the leaders time for one-on-one and group talks, including at an official dinner on Thursday that will be followed by a 2100 GMT news conference.
Blair and Jospin will take to the podium on Friday morning.

Analysts did not expect the changing face of Europe to make much difference to the European agenda which will continue to centre on EU enlargement, completing the IGC (EU Inter-Governmental Conference on institutional reform), and monetary union.
However social issues could be put more in the spotlight.
"There will be a great emphasis on the problems of unemployment and the underprivileged in all societies," said Olof Ruin, politics professor at the University of Stockholm.
"Environmental questions could also come up more often...and the whole question of immigration and what to do with ethnic and religious conflicts.
"I also think the scepticism prevailing in Social Democrat circles regarding EU membership will be somewhat changed."
The French Socialists' stance towards Europe's single currency, the euro, which has not been made clear since last weekend's election, is expected by many to be a focus.
"But the French are very interested in getting the euro so the differences will be less than one might expect," said one Western diplomat.
